claim: Accurate control of the cell cycle is critical for development and tissue homeostasis.
source: Accurate control of the cell cycle is critical for development and tissue homeostasis, and requires precisely timed expression of many genes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cell cycle importance.

claim: Cell cycle gene expression is regulated through transcriptional and translational control, as well as through regulated protein degradation.
source: Cell cycle gene expression is regulated through transcriptional and translational control, as well as through regulated protein degradation.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific consensus about mechanisms of cell cycle gene regulation.

claim: Two waves of mRNA decay occur sequentially during the mitosis-to-G1 phase transition.
source: We find that two waves of mRNA decay occur sequentially during the mitosis-to-G1 phase transition, and we identify the deadenylase CNOT1 as a factor that contributes to mRNA decay during this cell cycle transition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including spline analysis and RT-qPCR validation.

claim: CNOT1 contributes to mRNA decay during the mitosis-to-G1 phase transition.
source: We find that two waves of mRNA decay occur sequentially during the mitosis-to-G1 phase transition, and we identify the deadenylase CNOT1 as a factor that contributes to mRNA decay during this cell cycle transition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from CNOT1 depletion experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Scheduled mRNA decay helps to reshape cell cycle gene expression as cells move from mitosis into G1 phase.
source: Collectively, our data show that, akin to protein degradation, scheduled mRNA decay helps to reshape cell cycle gene expression as cells move from mitosis into G1 phase.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data and modeling presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Errors in cell cycle control may contribute to carcinogenesis.
source: Precise control over cell division is paramount, as errors may contribute to carcinogenesis (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Malumbres and Barbacid, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The cell cycle in somatic cells consists of four phases: G1, S, G2, and M phase.
source: The cell cycle in somatic cells consists of four phases: (1) in G1 phase a cell grows and prepares for DNA replication; (2) in S phase the DNA is replicated; (3) in G2 phase a cell prepares for segregation of the replicated genome; (4) in M phase (or mitosis) the cell divides and can then either enter into G1 phase of the next cell cycle or it can (temporarily) exit the cell cycle and enter into G0 phase (i.e. quiescence).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the cell cycle.

claim: Progression through the cell cycle is accompanied by the periodic expression of many genes.
source: Progression through the cell cycle is accompanied by the periodic expression of many genes (referred to as cell cycle genes), whose protein products are likely required in a particular cell cycle phase (Bar-Joseph et al., 2008; Chaudhry et al., 2002; Cho et al., 2001; Cho et al., 1998; Grant et al., 2013; Whitfield et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Reduced expression of G2 and M phase cell cycle genes impedes mitotic entry and affects the fidelity of chromosome segregation.
source: For instance, reduced expression of G2 and M phase cell cycle genes impedes mitotic entry and affects the fidelity of chromosome segregation (Laoukili et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Failure to suppress expression of G2 and M phase genes as cells enter G1 phase can result in a shortened G1 phase and cause DNA replication errors.
source: Conversely, a failure to suppress expression of G2 and M phase genes as cells enter G1 phase can result in a shortened G1 phase and cause DNA replication errors (García-Higuera et al., 2008; Park et al., 2008; Sigl et al., 2009), and can even contribute to carcinogenesis (Bortner and Rosenberg, 1997; Coelho et al., 2015; Kalin et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2006; Vaidyanathan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Scheduled protein degradation plays an important role in repression of cell cycle gene expression.
source: Scheduled protein degradation plays an important role in repression of cell cycle gene expression by ensuring that protein expression is restricted to the appropriate cell cycle phase (Nakayama and Nakayama, 2006; Vodermaier, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cells prevent de novo synthesis of proteins through inhibition of transcription to restrict protein expression to the correct cell cycle phase.
source: In addition, cells prevent de novo synthesis of proteins through inhibition of transcription to further restrict protein expression to the correct cell cycle phase (Bertoli et al., 2013; Sadasivam and DeCaprio, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Control of mRNA translation contributes to the regulation of gene expression during the cell cycle.
source: Indeed, control of mRNA translation also contributes to the regulation of gene expression during the cell cycle (Kronja and Orr-Weaver, 2011) and several hundreds of genes are subject to translational regulation at different phases of the cell cycle (Stumpf et al., 2013; Tanenbaum et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CLB2 and SWI5 mRNAs were shown to be degraded during mitosis in yeast.
source: Specifically, CLB2 and SWI5 mRNAs were shown to be degraded during mitosis (Trcek et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Several hundred genes show periodic changes in mRNA synthesis and degradation rates during the yeast cell cycle.
source: Globally, mRNA synthesis and decay rates during the cell cycle of yeast were derived through metabolic mRNA labeling in synchronized populations, resulting in the identification of several hundred genes that show periodic changes in mRNA synthesis and degradation rates (Eser et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The transcription factor ERG controls the degradation of a set of mRNAs during S phase.
source: For instance, the transcription factor ERG was shown to control the degradation of a set of mRNAs during S phase (Rambout et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Global mRNA synthesis and degradation rates during the human cell cycle were recently determined.
source: Recently, global mRNA synthesis and degradation rates during the human cell cycle were determined (Battich et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Pulse-chase approaches require relatively long measurement times (up to 6 hr), making accurate dynamics and rapid changes around cell cycle transition points difficult to determine.
source: However, due to the relatively long measurement time required for pulse-chase approaches (up to 6 hr), accurate dynamics and rapid changes, especially around the transition points in the cell cycle, are difficult to determine.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing methods based on general knowledge of the technique.

claim: The authors established a method that combines single-cell mRNA sequencing and live-cell imaging of cell cycle progression to map transcriptome-wide mRNA expression levels with high temporal resolution during the cell cycle.
source: To obtain a highly quantitative view of transcriptome dynamics during cell cycle phase transitions, we established a method that combines singe-cell mRNA sequencing and live-cell imaging of cell cycle progression to map transcriptome-wide mRNA expression levels with high temporal resolution during the cell cycle.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach developed in this study.

claim: The M-G1 phase transition was selected for study because gene expression needs to be 'reset' after cell division, requiring major changes to gene expression.
source: This cell cycle phase transition was selected as gene expression needs to be 'reset' after cell division, requiring major changes to gene expression.
evidence: This is the rationale for focusing on the M-G1 transition.

claim: Widespread protein degradation occurs during the M-G1 phase transition and is thought to contribute to resetting gene expression.
source: The widespread protein degradation that occurs during the M-G1 phase transition is thought to contribute to this reset (Castro et al., 2005; Harper et al., 2002; Peters, 2002; Vodermaier, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The first wave of mRNA decay is initiated during mitosis.
source: Using our method, we identified two temporally distinct waves of mRNA decay: the first wave is initiated during mitosis and the second wave is initiated within the first hours of G1 phase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including spline analysis and RT-qPCR validation.

claim: The second wave of mRNA decay is initiated within the first hours of G1 phase.
source: Using our method, we identified two temporally distinct waves of mRNA decay: the first wave is initiated during mitosis and the second wave is initiated within the first hours of G1 phase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including spline analysis and RT-qPCR validation.

claim: CNOT1 is a subunit of the CCR4-NOT mRNA deadenylase complex that shortens the poly(A) tail of mRNAs, generally resulting in their decay.
source: For several of these genes, we show that mRNA decay is stimulated by CNOT1, a subunit of the CCR4-NOT mRNA deadenylase complex that shortens the poly(A) tail of mRNAs, generally resulting in their decay (Garneau et al., 2007; Yamashita et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CNOT1 function, supported by citations.

claim: In the FUCCI system, an orange fluorescent protein (FUCCI-G1) is expressed in G1 and early S phase cells, as well as in G0 phase.
source: In the FUCCI system an orange fluorescent protein (FUCCI-G1) is expressed in G1 and early S phase cells, as well as in G0 phase (quiescence), while a green fluorescent protein (FUCCI-G2) is expressed in late S, G2, and early M phase (Figure 1A–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 1—video 1; Sakaue-Sawano et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the FUCCI system properties, supported by citation and figures.

claim: A green fluorescent protein (FUCCI-G2) is expressed in late S, G2, and early M phase.
source: In the FUCCI system an orange fluorescent protein (FUCCI-G1) is expressed in G1 and early S phase cells, as well as in G0 phase (quiescence), while a green fluorescent protein (FUCCI-G2) is expressed in late S, G2, and early M phase (Figure 1A–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 1—video 1; Sakaue-Sawano et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the FUCCI system properties, supported by citation and figures.

claim: FUCCI-G1 fluorescence intensity increases monotonically during the first 6–8 hr after G1 entry.
source: We used live-cell microscopy to measure FUCCI-G1 fluorescence intensity in cells as they progressed through G1 phase, which revealed a monotonic increase during the first 6–8 hr after G1 entry (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Cell cycle times of individual cells can be accurately determined during the first ~5 hr of G1/G0 phase using FUCCI-G1 fluorescence.
source: Cell cycle times of individual cells can be accurately determined during the first ~5 hr of G1/G0 phase, after which prediction accuracy decreases due to the increased cell-to-cell heterogeneity in FUCCI-G1 fluorescence at later time points in G1 phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of microscopy data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: 220 genes were downregulated when cells from G2/M phase were compared with G1 phase cells.
source: This analysis identified 220 genes that were downregulated and 42 genes that were upregulated when cells from G2/M phase were compared with G1 phase cells (using a cutoff of >2-fold expression change, see Materials and methods) (Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on differential transcriptome analysis of sequencing data.

claim: 42 genes were upregulated when cells from G2/M phase were compared with G1 phase cells.
source: This analysis identified 220 genes that were downregulated and 42 genes that were upregulated when cells from G2/M phase were compared with G1 phase cells (using a cutoff of >2-fold expression change, see Materials and methods) (Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on differential transcriptome analysis of sequencing data.

claim: Differentially expressed genes identified in the study were strongly enriched for cell cycle functions.
source: Gene Ontology analysis revealed that these differentially expressed genes were strongly enriched for cell cycle functions, as expected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology analysis of the sequencing data.

claim: Approximately 53% of all genes involved in the cell cycle are downregulated in early G1 phase.
source: Of all genes involved in the cell cycle (derived from Cyclebase 3.0; Santos et al., 2015), for which we could determine the expression, ∼53% is downregulated in early G1 phase in our dataset (>2-fold) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the sequencing data compared to known cell cycle genes.

claim: There was a large overlap between the differentially expressed genes identified by Monocle2 and the FUCCI-based method.
source: There was a large overlap between the differentially expressed genes identified by Monocle2 and our FUCCI-based method (Figure 1F), and we found a good overall correlation between FUCCI-based ordering and Monocle2-based ordering of G1 phase cells (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1M).
evidence: This is based on comparison of results from two different analysis methods.

claim: Monocle2 computed larger time intervals between cells early in G1 phase compared to the FUCCI-based method.
source: In general, Monocle2 computed larger time intervals between cells early in G1 phase compared to our FUCCI-based method (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is based on comparison of pseudo time assignments from Monocle2 with FUCCI-based cell cycle times.

claim: Transcriptome changes are larger in early G1 phase than at the end of G1 phase.
source: As Monocle2 computes the time intervals between cells based on the magnitude of transcriptome changes, a possible explanation for this observation is that transcriptome changes are larger in early G1 phase than at the end of G1 phase, and Monocle2 thus positions cells in early G1 phase too far apart in (pseudo) time.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Monocle2 and FUCCI-based timing.

claim: The first wave of mRNA decline occurred within 20 min of metaphase.
source: The first 'wave' of mRNA decline occurred within 20 min of metaphase (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1), which is around the time of mitotic exit, but before the start of G1 phase (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on spline analysis of the sequencing data.

claim: The second wave of mRNA decline occurred at ~80 min after metaphase.
source: The second wave occurred at ~80 min after metaphase (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1), which is in G1 phase (G1 phase starts between 15 and 30 min after metaphase; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on spline analysis of the sequencing data.

claim: mRNAs in the immediate decrease group declined most rapidly during the M-G1 phase transition and continued to decline during the first 2–3 hr of G1 phase.
source: Plotting the average slope over time for both groups revealed that the mRNAs in the immediate decrease group declined most rapidly during the M-G1 phase transition and continued to decline during the first 2–3 hr of G1 phase (Figure 2B, red lines), whereas the mRNAs in the delayed decrease group mostly declined between 1 and 4 hr after the start of G1 phase (Figure 2B, blue lines).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the sequencing data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: mRNAs in the delayed decrease group mostly declined between 1 and 4 hr after the start of G1 phase.
source: Plotting the average slope over time for both groups revealed that the mRNAs in the immediate decrease group declined most rapidly during the M-G1 phase transition and continued to decline during the first 2–3 hr of G1 phase (Figure 2B, red lines), whereas the mRNAs in the delayed decrease group mostly declined between 1 and 4 hr after the start of G1 phase (Figure 2B, blue lines).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the sequencing data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Most mRNAs reached a new steady-state level at later times (>8 hr) in G1 phase.
source: For both groups, the slopes of individual mRNAs were mostly centered around zero at later times (>8 hr) in G1 phase, demonstrating that most mRNAs reached a new steady-state level at later time points in G1 phase.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the sequencing data.

claim: RT-qPCR validation confirmed two distinct waves of mRNA decline.
source: Consistent with the RNA sequencing data, we observed two distinct waves of mRNA decline by RT-qPCR (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR experiments validating the sequencing results.

claim: TOP2A and CDK1 mRNA levels significantly decrease as early as anaphase.
source: Quantification of TOP2A and CDK1 mRNA levels at various stages of mitosis revealed a significant decrease in mRNA levels as early as anaphase, and a further decrease in telophase for both genes (Figure 2E–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: This is based on smFISH experiments shown in the referenced figures.

claim: TOP2A and CDK1 mRNA levels show a further decrease in telophase.
source: Quantification of TOP2A and CDK1 mRNA levels at various stages of mitosis revealed a significant decrease in mRNA levels as early as anaphase, and a further decrease in telophase for both genes (Figure 2E–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: This is based on smFISH experiments shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The levels of all five genes belonging to the immediate decrease group decline as cells move beyond metaphase.
source: RT-qPCR analysis revealed that the levels of all five genes belonging to the immediate decrease group decline as cells move beyond metaphase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR experiments shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The levels of all five transcripts belonging to the delayed decrease group do not decline between G2 phase, early and late mitosis.
source: In contrast, the levels of all five transcripts belonging to the delayed decrease group do not decline between G2 phase, early and late mitosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR experiments shown in the referenced figure.

claim: FBXO5 and UBE2C mRNA levels already show decline as cells move from G2 phase into early mitosis.
source: FBXO5 and UBE2C mRNA levels already show decline as cells move from G2 phase into early mitosis, while the levels of CDK1, TOP2A, and FZR1 mRNAs do not (their levels increase slightly between G2 phase and mitosis, which may reflect a cell synchronization artifact, as discussed before) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR experiments shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Both waves of mRNA decline occur in cells entering G1 phase (rather than G0).
source: We found that mRNA levels declined in two distinct waves (compare Figure 2—figure supplement 1M and Figure 2C), demonstrating that both waves of mRNA decline occur in G1 phase cells.
evidence: This is based on experiments in p53 knock-out cells that exclusively enter G1 after mitosis.

claim: Both waves of mRNA decline occur sequentially in the same cells.
source: We found that the expression levels of both groups of genes are highly correlated in individual cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1N), demonstrating that both waves of mRNA decline occur in the same cells.
evidence: This is based on single-cell analysis comparing expression of immediate and delayed decrease genes.

claim: Transcription is decreased for nearly all genes that are downregulated in G1 phase compared to G2/M phase.
source: Accordingly, comparison of transcription rates in G2 phase and G1 phase RPE-1 cells (data derived from Battich et al., 2020) shows that transcription is decreased for nearly all genes that are downregulated in G1 phase compared to G2/M phase (Figure 3A, see Materials and methods), regardless of whether mRNAs belong to the immediate decrease or delayed decrease group (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of previously published data.

claim: The onset of decay for different genes occurred most strongly at two distinct times during the M-G1 phase transition.
source: Using this approach, we confirmed that the onset of decay for different genes occurred most strongly at two distinct times during the M-G1 phase transition; either during the M-G1 phase transition or during early G1 phase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H), confirming the results from the spline analysis (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on mathematical modeling of the sequencing data.

claim: The median half-life of the 220 mRNAs downregulated in G1 phase is 61.5 min during the M-G1 phase transition.
source: This revealed a median half-life of 61.5 min in the decay phase during the M-G1 phase transition (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is based on mathematical modeling of the sequencing data.

claim: For almost all mRNAs (98–100%), the M-G1 half-lives computed are shorter than the reported half-lives of the same mRNAs in asynchronously growing cells.
source: For almost all mRNAs (98–100%) the M-G1 half-lives we computed are shorter than the reported half-lives of the same mRNAs in asynchronously growing cells (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1J-L; Herzog et al., 2017; Schwanhäusser et al., 2011; Tani et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on comparison of computed half-lives with previously published data.

claim: There are no significant differences between the half-lives of mRNAs belonging to the immediate decrease group versus the delayed decrease group.
source: We observed no significant differences between the half-lives of mRNAs belonging to the immediate decrease group versus the delayed decrease group (Figure 3—figure supplement 1M).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of computed half-lives.

claim: None of the 10 mRNAs tested showed an appreciable decrease in mRNA levels during 2 hr of transcription inhibition in mitosis.
source: None of the 10 mRNAs tested (belonging to both the immediate and delayed decrease groups) showed an appreciable decrease in mRNA levels during the 2 hr time window of Actinomycin D treatment, indicating that these mRNAs are much more stable in mitosis than they are during the M-G1 phase transition (Figure 3D, compare red or blue lines to gray line).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR experiments with transcription inhibition.

claim: For all genes tested, mRNA stability in G2 phase and late G1 phase substantially exceeded the mRNA stability calculated during the M-G1 phase transition.
source: For all genes tested, mRNA stability in G2 phase and late G1 phase substantially exceeded the mRNA stability calculated during the M-G1 phase transition (Figure 3E, compare red or blue lines to gray line).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR experiments with transcription inhibition.

claim: mRNAs are substantially more stable during G2 phase, mitosis (pre-anaphase), and late G1 phase compared to during the M-G1 phase transition and early G1 phase.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that for all genes tested, mRNAs are substantially more stable during G2 phase, mitosis (pre-anaphase), and late G1 phase compared to during the M-G1 phase transition and early G1 phase.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the transcription inhibition experiments.

claim: An active mRNA decay mechanism specifically takes place during mitotic exit and early G1 phase.
source: Thus, these results uncover an active mRNA decay mechanism that specifically takes place during mitotic exit and early G1 phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mRNA stability experiments.

claim: Cytoplasmic mRNA degradation is often initiated by shortening of the poly(A) tail.
source: Cytoplasmic mRNA degradation is often initiated by shortening of the poly(A) tail (Eisen et al., 2020), followed by degradation from either end of the mRNA (Garneau et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mRNA degradation mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Shortening of the poly(A) tail is frequently mediated by the CCR4-NOT complex.
source: Shortening of the poly(A) tail is frequently mediated by the CCR4-NOT complex (Yamashita et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: CNOT1 depletion resulted in substantially fewer mitotic cells and a strong enrichment of cells in G1 phase.
source: CNOT1 depletion resulted in substantially fewer mitotic cells and a strong enrichment of cells in G1 phase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), consistent with an important role for CNOT1 in cellular proliferation (Blomen et al., 2015; Hart et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on FACS analysis of CNOT1-depleted cells.

claim: Depletion of CNOT1 caused a 20–25% increase in the relative abundance of both TOP2A and CDK1 mRNAs in telophase compared to control cells.
source: In the mitotic cells that could be identified, depletion of CNOT1 caused a 20–25% increase in the relative abundance of both TOP2A and CDK1 mRNAs in telophase (when decay of these mRNAs has normally occurred) compared to control cells (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is based on smFISH experiments in CNOT1-depleted cells.

claim: CNOT1-dependent mRNA deadenylation is involved in mRNA decay at the M-G1 phase transition.
source: These results suggest that CNOT1-dependent mRNA deadenylation is involved in mRNA decay at the M-G1 phase transition.
evidence: This is inferred from the CNOT1 depletion experiments.

claim: The poly(A) tails of transcripts in the immediate decrease group were shorter than those of genes that did not show mRNA decay at the M-G1 phase transition (median value 58 versus 79).
source: Interestingly, re-analysis of this previous data revealed that the poly(A) tails of transcripts in the immediate decrease group were shorter than those of genes that did not show mRNA decay at the M-G1 phase transition (median value 58 versus 79, respectively) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on re-analysis of previously published data.

claim: The delayed decrease group mRNAs have significantly shorter poly(A) tails during mitosis than those in the control group (median value 75 versus 79).
source: The delayed decrease group mRNAs also have significantly shorter poly(A) tails during mitosis than those in the control group, although the effect was modest (median value 75 versus 79, respectively) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on re-analysis of previously published data.

claim: The shortened poly(A) tails were specific to mitosis, as poly(A) tail lengths in S phase of immediate and delayed decrease groups were similar to those of control genes.
source: Importantly, the shortened poly(A) tails were specific to mitosis, as poly(A) tail lengths in S phase of immediate and delayed decrease groups were similar to those of control genes (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on re-analysis of previously published data.

claim: CNOT1 aids the decay of TOP2A and CDK1 mRNAs during the M-G1 phase transition.
source: Collectively, these data show that CNOT1 aids the decay of TOP2A and CDK1 mRNAs during the M-G1 phase transition and suggest that CNOT1-dependent deadenylation in mitosis may contribute to the decay of many mRNAs at the M-G1 phase transition.
evidence: This is based on the CNOT1 depletion experiments and poly(A) tail analysis.

claim: CNOT1-dependent deadenylation in mitosis may contribute to the decay of many mRNAs at the M-G1 phase transition.
source: Collectively, these data show that CNOT1 aids the decay of TOP2A and CDK1 mRNAs during the M-G1 phase transition and suggest that CNOT1-dependent deadenylation in mitosis may contribute to the decay of many mRNAs at the M-G1 phase transition.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental data.

claim: A small but reproducible decrease in decay was observed for eight of the ten genes tested after CNOT1 depletion by CRISPRi.
source: Even though depletion of CNOT1 was modest in these experiments, a small but reproducible decrease in decay was observed for eight of the ten genes tested (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR experiments in CNOT1-depleted cells.

claim: Both waves of post-mitotic mRNA decay are stimulated by CNOT1.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that both waves of post-mitotic mRNA decay are stimulated by CNOT1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CNOT1 depletion experiments.

claim: Trajectory inference methods allow in silico ordering of cells based on (dis)similarities in transcriptomes.
source: To investigate transcriptome changes over time, trajectory inference methods have been developed that allow in silico ordering of cells, based on (dis)similarities in transcriptomes (Saelens et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about computational methods, supported by a citation.

claim: Pseudo time may under/overestimate true cellular state durations due to clustering based on transcriptome (dis)similarities.
source: However, due to clustering based on transcriptome (dis)similarities, pseudo time may under/overestimate true cellular state durations (Tian et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a known limitation of trajectory inference methods, supported by a citation.

claim: The FUCCI system has previously been used to order single-cell transcriptomes along the cell cycle.
source: Even though the FUCCI system has previously been used to order single-cell transcriptomes along the cell cycle (Battich et al., 2020; Hsiao et al., 2020; Mahdessian et al., 2021), a unique feature of our method is that it uses precisely calibrated FUCCI reporter fluorescence intensities for accurate assignment of cell cycle times of individual, sequenced cells.
evidence: This acknowledges previous work while highlighting the novelty of the current approach.

claim: The availability of temporal information allowed quantitative determination of mRNA degradation rates for transcripts.
source: The availability of temporal information allowed us to quantitatively determine mRNA degradation rates for these transcripts (Figure 3B–C and Supplementary file 1), which is not possible using trajectory inference methods.
evidence: This highlights an advantage of the FUCCI-based method over trajectory inference.

claim: The expression of G2/M-specific genes is reduced following the completion of cell division through scheduled protein degradation and transcriptional inactivation.
source: It is evident that the expression of G2/M-specific genes is reduced following the completion of cell division, both through scheduled protein degradation and transcriptional inactivation (Figure 3A; Bar-Joseph et al., 2008; Castro et al., 2005; Chaudhry et al., 2002; Cho et al., 2001; Cho et al., 1998; Grant et al., 2013; Harper et al., 2002; Nakayama and Nakayama, 2006; Peters, 2002; Vodermaier, 2004; Whitfield et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations and data from the current study.

claim: Widespread scheduled mRNA decay during mitotic exit and early G1 phase is an additional mechanism acting to reset gene expression following cell division.
source: Here, we identify widespread scheduled mRNA decay during mitotic exit and early G1 phase as an additional mechanism acting to reset gene expression following cell division.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: All the mRNAs tested are quite stable during mitosis and late G1 phase.
source: All the mRNAs we tested are quite stable during mitosis and late G1 phase (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is based on transcription inhibition experiments.

claim: Transcription inhibition by itself would lead to significant carry-over of transcripts into the next cell cycle.
source: Therefore, transcription inhibition by itself would lead to significant carry-over of transcripts into the next cell cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the mRNA stability data.

claim: Most mRNAs that are degraded during the M-G1 phase transition are not translationally repressed in G1 phase.
source: Therefore, decay-mediated clearance of mRNAs as cells exit mitosis could aid to limit expression of the encoded proteins in G1 phase, especially since most mRNAs that are degraded during the M-G1 phase transition are not translationally repressed in G1 phase (Tanenbaum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on previously published data cited in the text.

claim: Continued expression of G2/M genes in G1 phase may perturb normal cell cycle progression and potentially contribute to cellular transformation.
source: As these genes include many genes that encode for proteins with important functions in cell cycle control (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K), we speculate that their continued expression in G1 phase may perturb normal cell cycle progression, and potentially could even contribute to cellular transformation (García-Higuera et al., 2008; Park et al., 2008; Sigl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the data and previous literature.

claim: Scheduled mRNA decay during the cell cycle may be important to restrict gene expression of many cell cycle genes to their appropriate cell cycle phases.
source: Thus, scheduled mRNA decay during the cell cycle may be important to restrict gene expression of many cell cycle genes to their appropriate cell cycle phases.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The fact that mRNA decay occurs in two waves may indicate the existence of two distinct mechanisms that act consecutively to degrade transcripts.
source: The fact that mRNA decay occurs in two waves may indicate the existence of two distinct mechanisms that act consecutively to degrade transcripts.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed two waves of decay.

claim: Two waves of mRNA degradation during the M-G1 phase transition are highly reminiscent of the two consecutive waves of protein degradation that occur at the M-G1 transition.
source: Interestingly, these two waves of mRNA degradation during the M-G1 phase transition are highly reminiscent of the two consecutive waves of protein degradation that occur at the M-G1 transition (Alfieri et al., 2017; Sivakumar and Gorbsky, 2015).
evidence: This draws a parallel to known protein degradation patterns, supported by citations.

claim: RNA binding proteins can recruit components of the RNA decay machinery, such as the CCR4-NOT complex, to mRNA through direct interactions.
source: Through direct interactions with mRNAs, RBPs can recruit components of the RNA decay machinery, such as the CCR4-NOT complex, to the mRNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RNA regulation mechanisms.

claim: Recruitment of CCR4-NOT will induce deadenylation of the target transcript, generally followed by degradation.
source: Recruitment of CCR4-NOT, a key regulator of gene expression, will then induce deadenylation of the target transcript, generally followed by degradation (Garneau et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CCR4-NOT function, supported by a citation.

claim: The poly(A) tail lengths of genes identified as immediate decay are already shortened in early mitosis.
source: Interestingly, a previous report found that the poly(A) tail lengths of the genes we identified as immediate decay are already shortened in early mitosis (Figure 4B; Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on re-analysis of previously published data.

claim: CCR4-NOT-dependent deadenylation during early mitosis may mark transcripts for decay during mitosis and early G1 phase.
source: The observation that poly(A) tails of transcripts decayed during the M-G1 phase transition are shorter in mitosis could suggest that CCR4-NOT-dependent deadenylation during early mitosis marks these transcripts for decay during mitosis and early G1 phase.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the poly(A) tail data.

claim: The effects of CCR4-NOT depletion on mRNA decay are modest, likely caused by the inability to effectively deplete CNOT1 while maintaining cells in a cycling state.
source: We note that the effects of CCR4-NOT depletion on mRNA decay are modest in our experiments, but the magnitude of the effect is likely caused, at least in part, by the inability to effectively deplete CNOT1, while maintaining cells in a cycling state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental limitations.

claim: Additional mechanisms beyond CNOT1-dependent deadenylation may contribute to mRNA decay during the M-G1 phase transition.
source: Nonetheless, it is possible that additional mechanisms contribute to mRNA decay during the M-G1 phase transition.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential alternative mechanisms.

claim: Both waves of mRNA decay during the M-G1 phase transition are stimulated by CNOT1, but may be regulated independently involving distinct RBPs.
source: Our data shows that both waves of mRNA decay during the M-G1 phase transition are stimulated by CNOT1 (Figure 4D). Nonetheless, these waves of mRNA decay may be regulated independently, involving distinct RBPs.
evidence: This combines experimental data with speculative interpretation.

claim: Binding of distinct RBPs could ensure the timely decay of specific sets of mRNA during either mitotic exit or early G1 phase.
source: Binding of distinct RBPs could ensure the timely decay of specific sets of mRNA during either mitotic exit or early G1 phase.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential regulatory mechanisms.
